sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

questions.question: What did nurses want from the citations in the prior auth drafts?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted the citations to show them the specific chart entries the AI pulled from, rather than trusting a black-box summary. [1] They wanted to see "show your work" [2]

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
sources.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.

sources.title: Usability Test — AI-Assisted Prior Authorization Drafting (v1)
sources.participants: Participants: 4 — Utilization Review Nurse, Utilization Review Nurse (supervisor)
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Test whether an AI-drafted prior authorization request (pulling from chart data to pre-fill medical necessity justification) speeds up the process without introducing errors that could cause denials.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 4 realistic case scenarios, 60 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (accuracy) In 2 of 4 cases, the AI draft cited outdated diagnosis codes still present elsewhere in the chart rather than the most recent/active ones, which participants said would likely cause a payer denial if submitted as-is.
[HIGH] (liability concern) The supervisor was firm that nurses would still need to read every AI-drafted justification in full before submission, since a wrongly submitted prior auth can delay patient care by days — no shortcut is acceptable here.
[HIGH] (time savings (positive)) Despite the above, participants estimated the draft cut initial drafting time from ~15 minutes to ~5 minutes per straightforward case when the citation was correct, which was seen as a real win if accuracy improves.
[MEDIUM] (transparency) Participants wanted to see which specific chart entries the AI pulled from, inline, rather than trusting a black-box summary — 'show your work' was mentioned unprompted by 3 of 4.
Representative Quotes
"Five minutes saved is great until it's the case that gets denied and now I'm on the phone with the payer for 40 minutes instead. Show me where it got that info." — Utilization Review Nurse, P17
"I actually really liked this for the boring, obvious cases. Just don't let it near the complicated ones yet." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19
Recommendations
Fix the outdated-diagnosis-code issue before any further piloting; this is a correctness bug, not a UX issue.
Add inline source citations (chart entry + date) for every claim in the generated justification.
Consider limiting initial pilot scope to 'straightforward' case types the nurses themselves can help define, deferring complex cases.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Work with engineering to confirm whether the outdated-code issue is a data-freshness bug or a model retrieval issue.
Ask supervisor to help define what counts as a 'straightforward' case for a narrower v2 pilot scope.

sources.title: Usability Test — AI-Assisted Prior Authorization Drafting (v1)
sources.participants: Participants: 4 — Utilization Review Nurse, Utilization Review Nurse (supervisor)
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Test whether an AI-drafted prior authorization request (pulling from chart data to pre-fill medical necessity justification) speeds up the process without introducing errors that could cause denials.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 4 realistic case scenarios, 60 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (accuracy) In 2 of 4 cases, the AI draft cited outdated diagnosis codes still present elsewhere in the chart rather than the most recent/active ones, which participants said would likely cause a payer denial if submitted as-is.
[HIGH] (liability concern) The supervisor was firm that nurses would still need to read every AI-drafted justification in full before submission, since a wrongly submitted prior auth can delay patient care by days — no shortcut is acceptable here.
[HIGH] (time savings (positive)) Despite the above, participants estimated the draft cut initial drafting time from ~15 minutes to ~5 minutes per straightforward case when the citation was correct, which was seen as a real win if accuracy improves.
[MEDIUM] (transparency) Participants wanted to see which specific chart entries the AI pulled from, inline, rather than trusting a black-box summary — 'show your work' was mentioned unprompted by 3 of 4.
Representative Quotes
"Five minutes saved is great until it's the case that gets denied and now I'm on the phone with the payer for 40 minutes instead. Show me where it got that info." — Utilization Review Nurse, P17
"I actually really liked this for the boring, obvious cases. Just don't let it near the complicated ones yet." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19

Fix the outdated-diagnosis-code issue before any further piloting; this is a correctness bug, not a UX issue.
Add inline source citations (chart entry + date) for every claim in the generated justification.
Consider limiting initial pilot scope to 'straightforward' case types the nurses themselves can help define, deferring complex cases.

Work with engineering to confirm whether the outdated-code issue is a data-freshness bug or a model retrieval issue.
Ask supervisor to help define what counts as a 'straightforward' case for a narrower v2 pilot scope.

sources.title: Interview — Utilization Review Nurse on Checking Citations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
prior-authorization.md says nurses want inline citations to the chart text behind each part of the draft, and that in v2 the citations were used rather than ignored, with 3 of 4 participants clicking into at least one citation before accepting ( findings/prior-authorization.md :30-34). Both claims come from the April 2025 v1 and November 2025 v2 tests, whose participants asked for the citations or tested them. This session asked a utilization review nurse who joined the department after both tests, and has only ever used the panel in the pilot, whether they want the citations and how they check them, and how they handle the cases the panel doesn't take, including claim denials and calls with the health plan.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only; complex cases stay manual. The pilot is not generally available and has not reached other departments. The panel shows inline citations to the chart entries behind each part of the draft. The participant joined the department after the November 2025 v2 test and did not take part in any earlier session, so nothing here speaks to v1 or v2. They use the panel on their own straightforward cases. They are not P19, the utilization review nurse from v1 and June 2026, and not P17, the utilization review supervisor from v1 and v2. No pilot outcomes data was reviewed in this session, and the written straightforward-case definition was not reviewed either.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (citations as the way to read a draft) They want the citations, and don't think of them as an added feature: they have never used a draft without them, and opening them is how they read a draft at all. On each case they open the citation behind every criterion the request has to meet and read the chart entry it points to. What they check is whether that entry says what the draft says it says, not only that it exists; their example was a cited note that supports a symptom the draft describes as ongoing, when the note is months old. On their informal impression, most drafts need no change after checking and some need a sentence reworded; they kept no count. This confirms prior-authorization.md :30-34 for a nurse who wasn't in v1 or v2: the citations are wanted and used in pilot work, not only in testing. It also complicates the v2 measure: "clicked into at least one citation" records that a citation was opened, not what the nurse checked once it was.
[MEDIUM] (manual cases, claim denials and calls) Cases outside the pilot's straightforward scope they do by hand from the start. For a request that follows a claim denial, they begin from the denial letter's stated reason and then gather the chart evidence that answers it; in their view a draft built from the chart would start in the wrong place, because the reason is in the letter, not the chart. Before a call with the health plan about a case, they prepare by hand too, keeping their own list of chart references to have open during the call. They described the calls as the hardest part of the week to plan for, but gave no time figure. For a straightforward case that the health plan later asks about, they said they find the evidence again from scratch; they didn't know whether a submitted request keeps the panel's citations.
Representative Quotes
"I've never had a draft without them. The citations aren't extra, they're how I read the thing." — Utilization Review Nurse, P144
"A denial comes with a reason, and the reason's in the letter, not the chart. So I start from the letter and go find what answers it." — Utilization Review Nurse, P144
Recommendations
When prior-authorization.md is next revised, note that the citation requirement holds for a nurse who joined during the pilot, and that what they check is whether the cited text supports the draft's wording.
If citation use is measured in the pilot, record what nurses check in a citation, not only whether they open one.
Ask the pilot team whether a submitted request keeps its citations, so a nurse can reuse them if the health plan asks about the case later.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How the pilot is performing is not known: no outcomes data (time, accuracy, claim denials) is recorded in the corpus, none was reviewed here, and the participant had not seen any figures. The only time figures on record are v1's estimate and v2's measurement on 2 straightforward test cases.
Whether a submitted request keeps its citations is not known; the participant didn't know.
How many drafts need changing after the citations are checked is not counted; "most" needing no change is one nurse's impression.
Whether other pilot users check citations the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether drafting could help with requests that follow a claim denial is untested; the participant does them by hand, and nothing here supports bringing them into the pilot.

questions.question: How were sound-alike medication names handled?

seeded.answer:
The GA release candidate round (2026-01-13) treated sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing monitoring item, relying on the general confidence-highlighted variant to surface them. [1]

A concept test of a dedicated, visually distinct flag found 5 of 6 participants correctly recognized it as categorically different from generic low confidence — but also surfaced a new risk: 2 of 6 participants said the flag's specificity made them trust unflagged medication lines more than they should. [2]

One Physician (Family Medicine) checks every medication change in the plan against the order they placed, underlined or not, and rewrites changes worded as discussed rather than decided (2026-03-24, HIGH); they recalled one sound-alike name since GA, glyburide written where glipizide had been said, which was underlined, one recollection and not a rate (2026-03-24, MEDIUM). [3]

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient Scribe Sound-Alike Medication Flag Concept
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The GA-candidate round (2026-01-13) recommended treating sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing post-GA monitoring item rather than a launch blocker, since the existing confidence-highlighted variant already surfaces them as generically low-confidence. This session tests an early concept that goes one step further: a distinct flag specifically for suspected sound-alike medication names, visually separate from the general low-confidence underline, to see whether participants notice and act on it differently than they do on ordinary low-confidence text.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 6 simulated encounters seeded with known sound-alike pairs (e.g. hydralazine/hydroxyzine, clonidine/Klonopin), 40 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (flag recognized correctly) 5 of 6 participants correctly identified the medication-specific flag (a distinct amber pill-shaped badge, vs. the generic low-confidence underline) as "different from the usual low-confidence thing" within the first two encounters, without being told the distinction existed.
[MEDIUM] (over-trust risk) 2 participants said the badge's specificity made them more likely to treat unflagged medication lines as automatically correct — the opposite of the intended effect, and worth watching as adoption scales.
[LOW] (placement) Badge placement inline with the medication name (vs. in a right-hand margin, tested as an alternate) was preferred 5:1 — participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag.
[LOW] (false positive tolerance) One deliberately-seeded false positive (a real but unusual drug name) was accepted by all 6 participants as "worth a second look, not annoying" — suggests some over-flagging is tolerable if the badge is visually light.
Representative Quotes
"That's different from the fuzzy-underline stuff — this one's telling me specifically 'check the drug name,' which is exactly what I'd want flagged." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P22
"If it's not flagged, I might just... trust it more than I should. That's on me, but it's worth knowing the tool does that to people." — Nurse Practitioner, P24
Recommendations
Build the distinct medication-safety flag as its own variant, inline with the medication name, separate from generic confidence highlighting.
Before rollout, pair the flag with brief onboarding copy or training-pilot messaging that explicitly counters the over-trust-on-unflagged-lines risk surfaced by 2 of 6 participants — don't let the flag imply "anything unflagged is guaranteed correct."
Feed the false-positive tolerance finding to whoever tunes the sound-alike detection threshold — participants have headroom for a few extra false positives in exchange for not missing a real one.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Needs a larger-N validation pass before this moves from concept test to build-ready spec.
Over-trust-on-unflagged risk should be checked again once the post-GA monitoring dashboard (recommended 2026-01-13) has real error-rate data to compare against self-reported behavior.

Build the distinct medication-safety flag as its own variant, inline with the medication name, separate from generic confidence highlighting.

Needs a larger-N validation pass before this moves from concept test to build-ready spec.

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
[HIGH] (shared workstations) Two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
[MEDIUM] (framing) They described the lock as one more sign-in in a day full of them, not as a safety behavior. That matches the framing the 2026-02-17 inquiry recorded ("one more annoying re-login", 2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:45-48); it is this participant's own description, and the earlier finding was not put to them.
[MEDIUM] (what would help) Asked what they would want to see after a lock, without being shown anything, they said a message that the draft is saved and whose session it belongs to. That is an expectation; the paused state has not shipped and was not shown.
Representative Quotes
"I come back from the exam table and it's just sitting there. No message. I badge back in and scroll through before I say another word." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
"Two of us use that room. I don't know what happens to my recording if someone else taps in, so I stop it before I walk out." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
Recommendations
Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations

Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. questions.question: What time period does the ambient scribe GA adoption data cover?

seeded.answer: The first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout [1][2].

sources.title: Ambient Scribe GA Candidate — First 4 Weeks Adoption Topline
sources.excerpt:
Covers the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout, per the 2026-01-27 dashboard review ( raw/2026-01-27-dashboard-review-ambient-scribe-ga-adoption/ ).
Clinicians shown confidence highlighting skim high-confidence lines at roughly double the rate of the pre-highlighting cohort — directionally consistent with the GA-candidate usability finding that visible uncertainty, not raw accuracy, changes reviewing behavior.
Adoption is uneven by role: attending physicians are opting in at a noticeably higher rate than residents in the same departments.

sources.title: Dashboard review — Ambient scribe GA candidate adoption
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Manually review the internal usage dashboard for the ambient scribe GA release candidate to see whether adoption and engagement patterns in real usage match what the GA-candidate usability round found — particularly whether the per-line confidence highlighting is actually changing reviewing behavior at scale, not just in the moderated session.
Method
Method: Manual dashboard review (no moderated session, no participants) — internal analytics dashboard covering the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: none — this is an analytics review, not a research session; see participants.md in this folder for why
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (trust) Clinicians who were shown confidence highlighting skim high-confidence lines at roughly double the rate of the pre-highlighting cohort — directionally consistent with the usability round's finding that visible uncertainty, not raw accuracy, changes reviewing behavior.
[LOW] (adoption) Adoption is uneven by role: attending physicians are opting in at a noticeably higher rate than residents in the same departments, worth understanding qualitatively rather than assuming it's a training gap.
Recommendations
Feed this dashboard pattern back into findings/ambient-scribe.md as corroborating evidence for the confidence-highlighting result, rather than treating it as a separate finding.
Consider a short follow-up interview round specifically on the physician/resident adoption gap.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Is the physician/resident adoption gap explained by workflow differences, trust, or something else entirely? Dashboard data alone can't answer this.

questions.question: How aware were staff of the Compass AI initiatives?

seeded.answer: Only 34% of non-clinical staff reported being aware Compass AI initiatives were underway at all, versus 71% of clinical staff [1].

sources.title: Survey — All-Staff AI Readiness Pulse Survey
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Take an org-wide temperature check on AI readiness/sentiment heading into 2026, as input to roadmap prioritization and communications planning.
Method
Method: Org-wide anonymous pulse survey, 10 questions
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (awareness gap) Only 34% of non-clinical staff reported being aware Compass AI initiatives were underway at all, versus 71% of clinical staff — suggesting internal communications have been clinically focused and may need broadening if non-clinical rollouts (e.g., scheduling) proceed.
[MEDIUM] (sentiment trend (directional, not causal)) Among clinical respondents, favorable sentiment toward AI-assisted documentation was somewhat higher than the March-ish baseline period, though this survey used different question wording than February's, so it's directional context rather than a clean comparison.
[LOW] (top requested feature) When asked what AI feature they'd most want next, 'appointment scheduling help' was the top write-in among non-clinical/admin staff, and 'documentation time savings' remained the top pick among clinical staff — consistent with priorities identified all year.
Representative Quotes
"I hear about this AI stuff from clinical friends but nobody's told admin staff what's actually happening or if it affects us." — Non-clinical/administrative staff, P112 (survey open-ended)
Recommendations
Broaden internal communications about Compass AI to non-clinical staff specifically before any admin-facing pilot (e.g., scheduling chatbot) goes live, given the awareness gap found here.
If a clean sentiment trend is wanted for 2026 reporting, re-run the exact February nursing survey instrument rather than a new pulse survey, to get a true apples-to-apples comparison.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Decide with leadership whether the September burnout survey or a repeat of the February survey is the better instrument for the planned 6-month post-GA comparison.

Objective
Establish a pre-AI-rollout baseline of self-reported burnout and documentation burden, so future surveys can measure whether Compass AI tools move the needle.
Method
Method: Anonymous org-wide survey, 15 questions (validated burnout subscale + custom documentation items)
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (documentation as burnout driver) Documentation burden ranked as the #1 self-selected contributor to burnout among physicians specifically (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%).
[MEDIUM] (after-hours charting) 64% of physician respondents report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours ('pajama time'), averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours/day.
[MEDIUM] (baseline caution) Respondents were told this survey relates to a future AI initiative, which may have primed more favorable-than-baseline attitudes toward documentation-reducing tools — worth noting as a methodological caveat for anyone comparing to the February nursing survey, which didn't mention AI in its framing.

"I love this job. I do not love finishing my notes at 9pm after my kids are in bed. If AI fixes that, I'm in." — Physician, P84 (survey open-ended)
"Just don't let 'AI will fix documentation' become the excuse to skip fixing the actual EHR problems underneath it." — Nurse Practitioner, P91 (survey open-ended)
Recommendations
Use this survey as the official baseline metric for measuring Compass AI's impact on documentation burden and after-hours charting in future re-surveys (e.g., 6 and 12 months post-rollout).
Note the framing caveat explicitly in any report comparing this dataset to the February nursing survey.
Follow-ups / Open Questions

unseeded.answer:
Clinicians report that documentation burden is the #1 self-selected contributor to burnout among physicians specifically (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%) [1].

Sixty-four percent of physician respondents report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours ('pajama time'), averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours/day [1].

A rheumatologist interviewed in June 2026 said that many of their patients have long medication lists: disease-modifying drugs, a steroid, supplements, and drugs for other conditions managed by other clinicians. At most visits only one or two of those lines change. In the draft, a line that changed at this visit and a line that was only mentioned while going through the list look the same, and the underline marks only where the scribe was unsure what it heard. To find what changed they read the whole medication section against the orders they placed and the patient's current list. They put a long list at "fifteen lines, give or take" for many of their patients, an informal impression, not a count. [2]

They also said that in their account, dose changes in their clinic are often schedules rather than a single number: a prednisone taper stepped down over several weeks, or methotrexate taken once a week, where the day matters. They said the draft sometimes keeps the first step of a taper and drops the rest, or writes the methotrexate dose without "weekly". Those lines are usually not underlined, because each word was heard clearly. They rewrite the schedule by hand before signing. They put an incomplete taper at "a few times a month", an informal impression. [2]

sources.title: Interview — Rheumatologist on Medication Lines in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Earlier ambient-scribe sessions tested medication accuracy in drafts: dosage errors in v0.1 and v0.2 (2025-02-25-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v01/session-notes.md:30; 2025-09-23-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v02/session-notes.md:31), sound-alike drug names at the GA release candidate (2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate/session-notes.md:31), and a concept for a distinct sound-alike medication flag (2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/session-notes.md:21-27). Since GA, a family physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic described checking each medication change in the plan against the order they had placed (2026-03-24-interview-family-physician-plan-and-medication-changes-at-sign-off/session-notes.md:28, :32). No raw session dated on or before this one mentions a specialty clinic, rheumatology, a dose taper or a weekly dosing schedule. This session asked a rheumatologist, about six months after the January 2026 GA, how they check the medication lines in a draft when a patient's medication list is long and doses change often.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a rheumatologist in an ambulatory specialty clinic, mid-career. They opted in to the ambient scribe after the January 2026 GA and use it for most visits. The scribe drafts the visit note only; the clinician enters orders, including medication orders, separately. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. The distinct medication flag tested on 2026-02-10 has not shipped; there is no medication-specific marking beyond the confidence underline. They did not take part in any earlier session, and the researcher did not share what other participants had said. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (long lists) Many of their patients have long medication lists: disease-modifying drugs, a steroid, supplements, and drugs for other conditions managed by other clinicians. At most visits only one or two of those lines change. In the draft, a line that changed at this visit and a line that was only mentioned while going through the list look the same, and the underline marks only where the scribe was unsure what it heard. To find what changed they read the whole medication section against the orders they placed and the patient's current list. They put a long list at "fifteen lines, give or take" for many of their patients, an informal impression, not a count.
[HIGH] (dose schedules) In their account, dose changes in their clinic are often schedules rather than a single number: a prednisone taper stepped down over several weeks, or methotrexate taken once a week, where the day matters. They said the draft sometimes keeps the first step of a taper and drops the rest, or writes the methotrexate dose without "weekly". Those lines are usually not underlined, because each word was heard clearly. They rewrite the schedule by hand before signing. They put an incomplete taper at "a few times a month", an informal impression.
[MEDIUM] (whose dose) Patients often say what they actually take, which can differ from what was prescribed ("I've been taking half"). The draft records the dose that was said without saying who said it, so a patient's report can read like the clinician's decision. They check whether each dose in the draft is what the patient reported or what they decided, and reword it so the note says which. This is one rheumatologist's practice; whether other clinicians make the same check is not known.
[LOW] (what would help) Asked what would help, without being shown anything, they said a way to see which medication lines changed at this visit. That is an expectation; nothing was shown, and the distinct medication flag was not discussed with them.
Representative Quotes
"Fifteen medications and one of them changed today. The draft doesn't tell me which one, so I read all fifteen." — Physician (Rheumatology), P149
"It got the first dose right. The rest of the taper just isn't there." — Physician (Rheumatology), P149
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that, in this rheumatologist's account, multi-step dose schedules (tapers, weekly dosing) are where medication lines go wrong without being underlined, because each word is heard clearly.
When drafts are evaluated, include specialty-clinic visits with long medication lists and multi-step dose schedules, not only single dose changes.
Explore, as an open design question, whether a draft could show which medication lines changed at this visit and whether a dose is the patient's report or the clinician's decision; neither has been designed or tested.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often a dose schedule is written incompletely is not measured; "a few times a month" is one rheumatologist's impression.
Whether other specialists, or NPs and PAs in specialty clinics, check medication lines the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the distinct medication flag, which targets sound-alike names, would help with dose schedules is untested; it has not shipped.

questions.question: Why didn't physicians trust the ambient scribe's draft notes?

seeded.answer:
Physicians expressed concerns about the accuracy of the ambient scribe's drafts, particularly regarding the order of events in the history of present illness. [1][2]

They noted that while the scribe accurately captured individual words, it sometimes got the sequence of events wrong. [1][2]

Physicians also mentioned that they needed to read the entire draft, even if it was underlined in places, to ensure accuracy. [3][2]

sources.title: Interview — Returning Internal Medicine Physician on Edits and Trust Over Time
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P09 — Physician, Internal Medicine (physician), returning from 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The participant is P09, returning from 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate. In the v0.1 test they said they had to read every word anyway (2025-02-25-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v01/session-notes.md:36-37). In the v0.2 test they said they still read every line, and that getting it right once didn't mean they trusted it yet (2025-09-23-usability-test-ambient-scribe-v02/session-notes.md:36-37). At the GA release-candidate round they said it was the first time they had skimmed a section instead of reading every word, because it showed them where to look (2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate/session-notes.md:36-37); that round recorded 4 of 6 participants saying the per-line underline let them skim high-confidence lines (same file, :30). This interview is in September 2026. The questions were what they edit in drafts now, what they read in full and what they skim, and what in their account has changed or stayed the same since January.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an internal medicine physician in an ambulatory clinic. They have used the ambient scribe since the January 2026 GA. The scribe drafts the visit note only; they review the draft, correct single lines in place, and sign. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. Their earlier sessions were moderated usability tests; this is an interview about their own practice, nothing was shown or observed, and what they describe can't be compared directly with what those tests recorded. The researcher did not share what other participants had said.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (order of events) In their account, most of their edits now are not misheard words. The draft sometimes gets the order of events in the history wrong: which symptom came first, or how long ago something started. Those lines are usually not underlined, because each word was heard clearly. They put it at "a few notes most weeks", an informal impression, not a count.
[MEDIUM] (what they skim) They still skim history sections where nothing is underlined on routine follow-up visits, and read the assessment and plan in full on every draft. In January they said they skimmed a section for the first time instead of reading every word, because it showed them where to look (2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate/session-notes.md:36); what they read in full that day is not recorded, so the two can't be compared line by line.
[MEDIUM] (new problems) After catching, during review in the spring, a draft whose history put two symptoms in the wrong order with nothing underlined, they began reading the whole history whenever a visit is about a new problem. That is their account of a change in their own practice since January, not an observed change.
[MEDIUM] (trust by section) Asked whether they trust the scribe more than in January, they said it depends on the section: they rely on it to have heard the words, and they check that the history and the plan say what happened and what they decided. They did not describe their trust as having grown overall, and this interview does not measure trust.
[LOW] (edit count) They put their edits at "one or two on most notes", an informal estimate.
Representative Quotes
"It hears the words. What I check is whether the story's in the right order." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P09 (returning from 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate)
"Do I trust it more than in January? For some sections. Not the plan, and not the history of a new problem." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P09 (returning from 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate)
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that, in this physician's account, the order of events in the history is where drafts go wrong without being underlined, because each word is heard clearly.
When drafts are evaluated, check the sequence of events in the history against the visit, not only word accuracy.
If the team wants to know whether review habits change over time, plan a measure for it; one returning participant's account can't show a trend.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often the order of events is wrong is not measured; "a few notes most weeks" is one physician's impression.
Whether other clinicians read the history in full for new problems is not known; this is one interview.
Whether skimming has changed since January is not measured; the January round was a moderated test and this is an interview.

sources.title: Interview — Primary Care Physician on Incidental Content in Scribe Drafts
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Earlier ambient-scribe research looked at what the scribe gets wrong: medication dosages and sound-alike drug names, and whether clinicians trust the draft enough to skim it. Two sessions touched on what the scribe takes in more broadly. In an October 2025 contextual inquiry, a behavioral health clinician said that any AI tool listening to or drafting behavioral health session notes raises consent and 42 CFR Part 2 questions (2025-10-07-contextual-inquiry-behavioral-health-sensitive-notes/session-notes.md:28); the exclusion of that population from the near-term ambient scribe rollout is recorded in the scope-boundaries finding (scope-boundaries-and-workflow-fit.md:72-74). A care coordinator said the visit notes they read since GA are longer and more conversational than the notes clinicians used to type (2026-03-03-interview-care-coordinator-chart-review-scribe-notes/session-notes.md:31). Neither asked the person signing a draft about content the scribe writes down correctly but that doesn't belong in a visit note: small talk, a patient's remarks about other people, side conversations with a family member in the room. This session asked a primary care physician, two months after the January 2026 GA, what of that kind ends up in their drafts and what they remove before they sign.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an internal medicine physician in an ambulatory primary care clinic, mid-career. They opted in to the ambient scribe after the January 2026 GA and use it for most of their visits. The scribe drafts visit notes for physicians, NPs and PAs; the clinician reviews the draft, corrects single lines in place, and signs. Low-confidence transcription is shown with a subtle underline. They did not take part in any earlier session. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (incidental content) Their drafts regularly contain things that were said in the room but that they would not have written themselves: small talk at the start of the visit, a patient's remarks about a relative's health, comments made by a family member who came to the visit, and their own asides ("let me pull up your labs"). They remove these line by line with the in-place edit before signing. They put it at "most visits, a line or two", an informal impression, not a count.
[MEDIUM] (not underlined) The underline marks lines where the scribe was unsure what it heard. Incidental content is usually transcribed accurately, so it is not underlined, and nothing in the draft points them to it. It also doesn't land in a predictable section: they have found it in the history of present illness and in the social history. To catch it they read the whole draft, including sections where nothing is underlined. That is one physician's practice; whether others do the same is not known.
[MEDIUM] (judgement) What counts as incidental is a judgement call. A remark about stress at home can be clinically relevant and stay in the note; the same remark in passing about someone else is removed. They would not want the scribe to remove anything on its own. They could see value in it pointing out lines that might not belong, as long as they decide. That is an expectation; nothing was shown.

"It writes down everything that was said, not everything that matters. The sister's surgery is in my note until I take it out." — Physician (Internal Medicine), P146

sources.title: Interview — Medical Coder on Coding from AI-Drafted Notes
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Two months after the ambient scribe went GA in January 2026, understand how coding from scribe-drafted notes differs from coding notes the physician typed, and what a coder would expect from the AI coding-suggestion concept (tested as a prototype in July 2025, not built or piloted) now that much of the documentation it would read is itself AI-drafted.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: Participant codes outpatient and some inpatient encounters daily and has coded from scribe-drafted notes since GA. They did not take part in the July 2025 usability test; their view of the coding-suggestion concept comes from a walkthrough of the July 2025 screens during this session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (documentation gaps) Scribe-drafted notes often capture what was discussed in the visit but leave out the specificity coding depends on: laterality, acute vs. chronic, type or stage (they gave heart failure type and CKD stage as examples), and the "due to" link between two conditions. When it's missing the coder has two options, query the physician or code to the unspecified level, and they said they are doing both more often than with notes physicians typed from their own templates. They noted the July 2025 prototype's mismatches were mostly at the specificity level too, and expect a suggester reading these notes to hit the same wall.
[MEDIUM] (trust in AI-drafted notes) Nothing in the signed note shows which sentences the scribe drafted and which the physician typed or edited. When a sentence looks off (e.g., a diagnosis in the assessment that nothing else in the note supports), the coder can't tell whether it's a documentation problem worth a query or something the scribe picked up from the conversation that the physician didn't catch at sign-off. They weren't asking for a marker on the permanent chart, just "something I can see while I'm coding".
[MEDIUM] (query volume) Coder's impression is that queries back to physicians have gone up since GA, and that physicians are slower to answer queries about notes "they didn't really write". This is qualitative only: they had no count, and no department query data was reviewed in this session.
Representative Quotes
"I'm coding off what the doctor says happened. Now I read a sentence and I honestly don't know if the doctor said it or the scribe thing filled it in. Who wrote this? I can't tell you, and I'm the one putting a code on it." — Medical Coder (certified), P120
"If the suggester is reading the same notes I'm reading, it's going to land on unspecified too. It'll just get there faster than me." — Medical Coder (certified), P120
Recommendations
Collect the specificity elements coders most often query on scribe-drafted notes (laterality, acuity, type/stage, condition linkage) and share them with the ambient scribe team as input to the drafting prompts and note structure.
For the coding-suggestion concept, design for under-specified input: when the note doesn't support a specific code, the tool should say so rather than quietly suggest the unspecified code.
Raise with Compliance whether scribe-drafted vs. clinician-edited provenance could be shown in the coding view only, consistent with the CMIO's August 2025 model of no marker on the permanent chart.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Get actual physician query counts from HIM leadership for the months before and after GA, to check the coder's impression.
Find out whether the scribe's generation metadata is captured at sentence level, and whether it could reach the coding workflow at all.

Physicians expressed concerns about the accuracy of the ambient scribe's drafts, particularly regarding the order of events in the history of present illness. [1][2]

They noted that while the scribe accurately captured individual words, it sometimes got the sequence of events wrong. [1][2] This led to a need for physicians to carefully review the entire history section, even on routine follow-up visits, to ensure the accuracy of the narrative. [2]

Physicians also mentioned that they still needed to read the entire assessment and plan sections in every draft, indicating a lack of complete trust in the scribe's ability to accurately capture these critical elements. [2]

questions.question: What did nurses want from the AI's citations?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted the citations to show them the specific chart text behind each part of the AI-generated draft. [1][2] They used the citations to check whether the draft accurately reflected the chart entries. [2]

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
sources.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.

sources.title: Interview — Utilization Review Nurse on Checking Citations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
prior-authorization.md says nurses want inline citations to the chart text behind each part of the draft, and that in v2 the citations were used rather than ignored, with 3 of 4 participants clicking into at least one citation before accepting ( findings/prior-authorization.md :30-34). Both claims come from the April 2025 v1 and November 2025 v2 tests, whose participants asked for the citations or tested them. This session asked a utilization review nurse who joined the department after both tests, and has only ever used the panel in the pilot, whether they want the citations and how they check them, and how they handle the cases the panel doesn't take, including claim denials and calls with the health plan.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only; complex cases stay manual. The pilot is not generally available and has not reached other departments. The panel shows inline citations to the chart entries behind each part of the draft. The participant joined the department after the November 2025 v2 test and did not take part in any earlier session, so nothing here speaks to v1 or v2. They use the panel on their own straightforward cases. They are not P19, the utilization review nurse from v1 and June 2026, and not P17, the utilization review supervisor from v1 and v2. No pilot outcomes data was reviewed in this session, and the written straightforward-case definition was not reviewed either.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (citations as the way to read a draft) They want the citations, and don't think of them as an added feature: they have never used a draft without them, and opening them is how they read a draft at all. On each case they open the citation behind every criterion the request has to meet and read the chart entry it points to. What they check is whether that entry says what the draft says it says, not only that it exists; their example was a cited note that supports a symptom the draft describes as ongoing, when the note is months old. On their informal impression, most drafts need no change after checking and some need a sentence reworded; they kept no count. This confirms prior-authorization.md :30-34 for a nurse who wasn't in v1 or v2: the citations are wanted and used in pilot work, not only in testing. It also complicates the v2 measure: "clicked into at least one citation" records that a citation was opened, not what the nurse checked once it was.
[MEDIUM] (manual cases, claim denials and calls) Cases outside the pilot's straightforward scope they do by hand from the start. For a request that follows a claim denial, they begin from the denial letter's stated reason and then gather the chart evidence that answers it; in their view a draft built from the chart would start in the wrong place, because the reason is in the letter, not the chart. Before a call with the health plan about a case, they prepare by hand too, keeping their own list of chart references to have open during the call. They described the calls as the hardest part of the week to plan for, but gave no time figure. For a straightforward case that the health plan later asks about, they said they find the evidence again from scratch; they didn't know whether a submitted request keeps the panel's citations.
Representative Quotes
"I've never had a draft without them. The citations aren't extra, they're how I read the thing." — Utilization Review Nurse, P144
"A denial comes with a reason, and the reason's in the letter, not the chart. So I start from the letter and go find what answers it." — Utilization Review Nurse, P144
Recommendations
When prior-authorization.md is next revised, note that the citation requirement holds for a nurse who joined during the pilot, and that what they check is whether the cited text supports the draft's wording.
If citation use is measured in the pilot, record what nurses check in a citation, not only whether they open one.
Ask the pilot team whether a submitted request keeps its citations, so a nurse can reuse them if the health plan asks about the case later.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How the pilot is performing is not known: no outcomes data (time, accuracy, claim denials) is recorded in the corpus, none was reviewed here, and the participant had not seen any figures. The only time figures on record are v1's estimate and v2's measurement on 2 straightforward test cases.
Whether a submitted request keeps its citations is not known; the participant didn't know.
How many drafts need changing after the citations are checked is not counted; "most" needing no change is one nurse's impression.
Whether other pilot users check citations the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether drafting could help with requests that follow a claim denial is untested; the participant does them by hand, and nothing here supports bringing them into the pilot.

sources.title: Interview — Utilization Review Nurse on Checking Citations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
prior-authorization.md says nurses want inline citations to the chart text behind each part of the draft, and that in v2 the citations were used rather than ignored, with 3 of 4 participants clicking into at least one citation before accepting ( findings/prior-authorization.md :30-34). This session asked a utilization review nurse who joined the department after both tests, and has only ever used the panel in the pilot, whether they want the citations and how they check them, and how they handle the cases the panel doesn't take, including claim denials and calls with the health plan.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only; complex cases stay manual. The pilot is not generally available and has not reached other departments. The panel shows inline citations to the chart entries behind each part of the draft. The participant joined the department after the November 2025 v2 test and did not take part in any earlier session, so nothing here speaks to v1 or v2. They use the panel on their own straightforward cases. They are not P19, the utilization review nurse from v1 and June 2026, and not P17, the utilization review supervisor from v1 and v2. No pilot outcomes data was reviewed in this session, and the written straightforward-case definition was not reviewed either.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (citations as the way to read a draft) They want the citations, and don't think of them as an added feature: they have never used a draft without them, and opening them is how they read a draft at all. On each case they open the citation behind every criterion the request has to meet and read the chart entry it points to. What they check is whether that entry says what the draft says it says, not only that it exists; their example was a cited note that supports a symptom the draft describes as ongoing, when the note is months old. On their informal impression, most drafts need no change after checking and some need a sentence reworded; they kept no count. This confirms prior-authorization.md :30-34 for a nurse who wasn't in v1 or v2: the citations are wanted and used in pilot work, not only in testing. It also complicates the v2 measure: "clicked into at least one citation" records that a citation was opened, not what the nurse checked once it was.
[MEDIUM] (manual cases, claim denials and calls) Cases outside the pilot's straightforward scope they do by hand from the start. For a request that follows a claim denial, they begin from the denial letter's stated reason and then gather the chart evidence that answers it; in their view a draft built from the chart would start in the wrong place, because the reason is in the letter, not the chart. Before a call with the health plan about a case, they prepare by hand too, keeping their own list of chart references to have open during the call. They described the calls as the hardest part of the week to plan for, but gave no time figure. For a straightforward case that the health plan later asks about, they said they find the evidence again from scratch; they didn't know whether a submitted request keeps the panel's citations.

"I've never had a draft without them. The citations aren't extra, they're how I read the thing." — Utilization Review Nurse, P144

If citation use is measured in the pilot, record what nurses check in a citation, not only whether they open one.

How the pilot is performing is not known: no outcomes data (time, accuracy, claim denials) is recorded in the corpus, none was reviewed here, and the participant had not seen any figures. The only time figures on record are v1's estimate and v2's measurement on 2 straightforward test cases.
Whether a submitted request keeps its citations is not known; the participant didn't know.
How many drafts need changing after the citations are checked is not counted; "most" needing no change is one nurse's impression.
Whether other pilot users check citations the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether drafting could help with requests that follow a claim denial is untested; the participant does them by hand, and nothing here supports bringing them into the pilot.

questions.question: How did Practice Administrators expect the invite step to work?

seeded.answer:
Three out of four Practice Administrators hesitated at the Invite your team step because they weren't sure when the email was sent: whether it was sent when they finished the step or at Review & finish [1][2][3].

They also didn't want staff emailed before champion training was booked for the practice [1][2][3].

sources.title: The Practice Administrator — Compass AI Practice Setup Journey
sources.excerpt:
Invite your team. In the test, 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated: unsure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and not wanting staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment (2026-02-03 :53 ). The step used a prepared test staff list, so no real staff were emailed ( :41-42 ).
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — P157 ( :64-65 )

sources.title: Wants to Know What a Step Commits Them To
sources.excerpt:
What it sends, and when. 3 of 4 Practice Administrators hesitated at Invite your team, unsure when the email goes out and not wanting staff emailed before champion training is booked ( :53 ). "If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — P157 ( :64-65 )
What it leaves them maintaining. P159 asked whether invites create accounts or use existing SSO groups: "if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." ( :54 , :70-71 )

sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
